report:
## Conclusion

The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism is **not supported by scientific evidence**. Large, high-quality studies consistently find no causal link, and the strongest counter-evidence comes from claims based on retracted or methodologically weak research.

## Evidence Review

The most robust recent evidence is a Danish cohort study of over 1.2 million children, which found "no compelling evidence to suggest that childhood vaccines could cause autism or other chronic health conditions," including no link between aluminum-containing vaccines and neurological, autoimmune, or allergic disorders (https://www.healthline.com/health-news/research-finds-no-evidence-vaccines-cause-autism). A comprehensive review echoes this, noting that "the great majority of scientists, physicians, and public health researchers" have refuted causation between vaccines and autism after extensive scrutiny (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8694782/).

Claims supporting a link often trace back to compromised sources. The original 1998 paper suggesting an MMR-autism connection was retracted due to fraud, as documented by Johns Hopkins (https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/vaccines-do-not-cause-autism). Subsequent "whistleblower" claims (the Hooker/Thompson CDC controversy) have been scrutinized by scientific commentators, who note the underlying data actually showed *reduced* autism odds among MMR-vaccinated children when analyzed properly, undermining suppression narratives (https://www.forbes.com/sites/emilywillingham/2014/05/15/vaccines-thimerosal-mmr-mercury-not-associated-with-autism/).

Studies claiming positive associations, such as ecological studies correlating vaccine schedule "intensity" with autism prevalence across countries, are methodologically weak—ecological studies cannot establish causation because they compare population-level trends rather than individual exposure and outcome, and cannot control for confounding factors like diagnostic changes over time.

**Bottom line:** The weight of rigorous, large-scale epidemiological evidence contradicts this claim. Your skepticism toward it is well-founded.
